ask: Why is it on the path?
cards: Miniature clay wheels from north of the Black Sea, from before 4000 BCE, are the oldest indirect evidence of wheeled movement; the spoked wheel later allowed swifter war chariots.
Speakers of Sumerian, with Egyptian one of the two earliest written languages, developed cuneiform around 3200 BCE, at first to keep accounts, on tablets written at Uruk.
In 105 CE this court eunuch of the Eastern Han presented Emperor He with paper made from tree bark, hemp, old rags and fishing nets, cheaper than silk and lighter than bamboo.
Developed in China, the magnetised needle was used for navigation at sea under the Song Dynasty, aided maritime trade and later transformed navigation worldwide.
Around 1040 CE this Song Dynasty artisan invented movable type printing with ceramic characters, a method recorded by the scholar Shen Kuo, about four centuries before Gutenberg.
In the fifteenth century Johannes Gutenberg developed printing with movable metal type in Europe, and his press transformed the spread of knowledge there.
From Copernicus in 1543 to Newton in 1687, European scholars joined mathematics, measurement and experiment and used new instruments such as the telescope, microscope and air pump.
Jerónimo de Ayanz patented a steam-powered mine pump in 1606, and Thomas Newcomen's engine of about 1712 was the first commercially successful one to transmit continuous power.
James Watt's separate condenser, patented in 1769, greatly reduced fuel use, and with Matthew Boulton at Birmingham from 1775 he built engines that drove mills and pumped mines.
Developed in the nineteenth century, the telegraph sent messages by electrical signals along wires, and submarine cables linked Britain with India, Australia and other parts of its empire.
